title: South Africa's asylum ruling unrest
dek: Riots in Durban and Soweto after a court ruling on asylum, the army deployment and arrests that followed, and the competing claims over what the ruling means and who is behind the violence.
summary: On July 7, 2026, South Africa's Constitutional Court struck down rules that barred people from applying for asylum if they had entered the country irregularly, had no asylum transit visa or missed a reporting deadline. On September 28 the Home Affairs department told refugee offices to accept in-person applications. The move came after months of protests by anti-migrant groups, which had demanded that undocumented foreigners leave.

In early October anti-migrant groups, including March and March, protested at refugee offices. On October 8 protests in Soweto and Durban turned violent: police say 24 vehicles were torched, and foreign-owned shops were looted. Home Affairs withdrew the directive on October 9, saying its offices had been overwhelmed, but violence continued in Durban and the army was deployed there on October 10. Officials say 30 people were arrested in the first days, and court cases are under way.

The government says the ruling has been misrepresented: it does not automatically grant refugee status, residence or voting rights, and officials blame deliberate false information for the violence. Anti-migrant groups say the ruling and directive opened the door to undocumented migrants, and March and March denies its members were behind the violence. Rights groups say the court order is binding and call for those who incited violence to be prosecuted. Local elections are due on November 4.

phases.name: Anti-migrant protests and the court ruling
The directive and the first protests
Arrests, courts and the government's plan

events.label: reported
events.text: Police say more than 900 people were arrested during anti-migrant protests, after groups set a June 30 deadline for undocumented foreigners to leave the country, Reuters reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The Constitutional Court rules that people cannot be barred from applying for asylum because they entered irregularly, had no asylum transit visa or missed a reporting deadline; officials must consider individual claims. The case was brought by the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town and Lawyers for Human Rights.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The Home Affairs director-general issues a directive telling refugee reception offices to accept in-person asylum applications.

events.label: reported
events.text: Members of the anti-migrant group March and March disrupt asylum processing at the Durban refugee reception office, Daily Maverick reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Home Affairs says a "coordinated disinformation campaign" is misrepresenting the ruling and says it will refer the matter to the Electoral Commission.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Protests in Soweto and Durban turn violent. Acting National Police Commissioner Puleng Dimpane says 24 vehicles were torched, 10 in Soweto and 14 in Durban, and foreign-owned shops are looted.

events.label: disputed
events.text: KwaZulu-Natal police say three foreign nationals were arrested on suspicion of attacking a protester and breaking his neck, and that this may have sparked the Durban violence. Protesters say a demonstrator was shot by a foreign national; in Soweto, a community leader alleges foreign nationals fired shots first.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Government spokesperson William Baloyi says the violence was triggered by people deliberately spreading false information, and that the ruling does not automatically give anyone refugee status or other rights. The inter-ministerial committee on migration says all refugee offices are overwhelmed.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Home Affairs withdraws the directive, saying its offices were "overwhelmed within a matter of days". The department says the directive was issued without Minister Leon Schreiber's knowledge; Schreiber says the department changed its position because the "facts shifted".

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Violence continues in Durban for a second day; AFP reports police using tear gas and stun grenades, houses set alight and shops looted. President Cyril Ramaphosa says the security cluster is handling the unrest and there should be no loss of life.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Protesters march to the Constitutional Court in Johannesburg. Daily Maverick reports police fired rubber bullets and a vehicle was set alight.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Soldiers are deployed in Durban and patrol the city centre with police, after KwaZulu-Natal Premier Thami Ntuli called for the army.

events.label: reported
events.text: KwaZulu-Natal police say 19 people have been arrested in Durban, four of them for attempted murder and discharging a firearm in public. March and March's founder says on social media that the group does not associate itself with criminal activities.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Police arrest three March and March members outside the Durban refugee office; they are charged with incitement to commit public violence, public violence and riotous or threatening conduct.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi, who chairs the inter-ministerial committee, says the government will ask the courts for a supervisory order on implementing the ruling, possibly with a suspension period. She says a new asylum appointment system will be in place by November 10 and that 30 people have been arrested since October 8.

events.label: reported
events.text: Nigeria's foreign ministry says 2,037 Nigerians have been repatriated from South Africa since June 10 amid what it calls xenophobic attacks.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: 24 accused appear in Durban Magistrate's Court. Two of the arrested March and March members are granted bail of R1,000 on condition they stay away from violent protests and from Home Affairs offices.

events.label: reported
events.text: TimesLIVE reports that a panel of Gauteng High Court judges, appointed by Judge President Aubrey Ledwaba, will hear the government's bid for court supervision of the asylum ruling on October 29; Kubayi says the hearing will consider submissions on how the ruling is implemented.

events.label: reported
events.text: Three Ethiopian nationals, aged 38, 48 and 29, appear in the Durban Magistrate's Court on attempted murder and public violence charges over the October 8 assault, which police say happened as a group marched to join March and March members outside the Durban refugee office. Police allege the men beat a South African man with sticks, stones and a bushknife and broke both his legs, a different injury from the broken neck police described on October 8; the state says they intended to kill him. They are remanded in custody, with the case due back on October 19.

events.label: reported
events.text: Lawyers for Human Rights says the government should not seek a supervisory order, arguing it waited months after the July ruling to seek legal advice, and says it is unclear whether papers have been filed, EWN reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The lawyer for March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma says arrest warrants have been issued for her and for him; the movement calls it intimidation before the elections. The National Prosecuting Authority and KwaZulu-Natal police say no warrant or case exists.

events.label: reported
events.text: IOL reports that 19 people linked to the movement appear in Durban Magistrate's Court on charges linked to public violence.

events.label: reported
events.text: Speaking at a Black Wednesday commemoration in Sandton, President Ramaphosa dismisses social media claims that the ANC is registering asylum seekers to vote as "a rubbish story," IOL reports. The Electoral Commission says asylum seeker status does not confer voting rights and that only South African citizens aged 18 or over on the voters' roll may vote in the November 4 local elections.

events.label: reported
events.text: A crowd of about 50 people beats an unidentified man, reported to be a foreign national, to death on Dr Pixley kaSeme Street in central Durban at around 7am on October 22 as he is walking to work; a witness says the crowd was targeting immigrants, GroundUp reports via Daily Maverick. KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Colonel Robert Netshiunda confirms a murder case has been opened; no suspects have been named.

events.label: reported
events.text: Protesters attack the VFS Global Home Affairs visa application centre in Berea and ransack a building near Problem Mkhize Road, IOL reports; KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Colonel Robert Netshiunda says police are working to identify those responsible. About 80% of central Durban shops remain closed.

events.label: reported
events.text: A Durban Magistrate's Court bail hearing for three foreign nationals charged with attempted murder and public violence over the October 8 attack on a protester is adjourned to October 28 and the men remain in custody, IOL reports. The state says the man was left with fractures to both legs; it opposes bail, citing community anger, the seriousness of the charges and flight risk, while the defence disputes that its client took part in the violence.

events.label: reported
events.text: The Electoral Commission tightens security for the November 4 KwaZulu-Natal local elections, adding police and contracted guards at voting stations and material warehouses and saying protesters "won't be tolerated anywhere near voting stations," TimesLive reports; the province has been on high alert for months over anti-migrant unrest, including the Durban killing reported on October 22.

events.label: reported
events.text: Police arrest five men, aged 19 to 46, outside the Home Affairs offices on Che Guevara Road in Umbilo as persons of interest in the murder, attempted murder and assault cases linked to the unrest, Netshiunda says, IOL reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: IOL reports that violent anti-immigration protests in Durban have escalated, with killings, looting and businesses ransacked.

events.label: pending
events.text: Local government elections on November 4, the October 29 court hearing on the government's supervisory-order bid, and the new asylum appointment system due by November 10. Still being checked.

claims.title: What does the court ruling do?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: The government says the ruling does not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or voting rights, and that false claims about it caused the violence.
claims.b: Anti-migrant groups say the ruling and the directive opened the door to undocumented migrants; March and March's founder called the ruling "absolutely shocking".
claims.status: The ruling requires officials to consider individual asylum claims and remains binding after the directive was withdrawn (Mail & Guardian).

claims.title: Who is responsible for the violence?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: March and March says it does not associate itself with criminal activities. Protesters say the Durban violence followed the alleged shooting of a demonstrator by a foreign national.
claims.b: Police say three foreign nationals were arrested over an assault on a protester, and dozens of people have been arrested for public violence. A coalition of 160 civil society groups calls for those who incited violence to be prosecuted.
claims.status: Court cases are under way; no court has made findings yet.

claims.title: Were arrest warrants issued for March and March leaders?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: The movement's lawyer says warrants were issued for him and the movement's founder; its spokesperson calls this intimidation before the November 4 elections.
claims.b: The National Prosecuting Authority and KwaZulu-Natal police say no warrant was issued and no case exists.
